title: Accessing electronic entanglement via photo-assisted two-electron tomography
authors: M. Paulet, G. Rebora, M. Bienioszek, G. Ménard, G. Fève, A. Feller, P. Degiovanni
abstract: Witnessing entanglement between electrons propagating in quantum circuits requires accessing their two-electron coherences, which encode the two-particle quantum correlations generated by Coulomb interactions. Yet, experimental reconstruction of two-electron coherence remains a major challenge. We introduce photo-assisted two-electron tomography, a quantum coherence reconstruction protocol from dc-currents and time-averaged current correlations, routinely measured in electron quantum optics experiments. Driving an energy filter with a small rf tone encodes off-diagonal coherences in the frequency domain into the dc-current response, enabling single-electron tomography without resorting to current-noise measurements. Extending it to two channels, current correlations after two photo-assisted filters reconstruct the two-electron Wigner distribution and isolate its irreducible two-body part. When applied to Coulomb-coupled quantum Hall edge channels, the protocol reveals interaction-induced energy entanglement. Signatures of this entanglement are visible through the violation of an entanglement witness based on Cauchy-Schwarz inequalities, as well as Wigner function negativities, which remain resolved above the thermal background for realistic device parameters. A generalized Franson geometry further extends the approach to intra-channel two-electron coherences. This opens a direct pathway to detect and characterize electronic entanglement in ballistic quantum circuits.
summary: This paper presents a novel 'photo-assisted two-electron tomography' protocol to measure two-electron coherences in quantum circuits using only standard current measurements. By applying this technique to quantum Hall edge channels, the authors demonstrate a direct method to detect and quantify interaction-induced electronic entanglement. This opens a powerful new experimental avenue for studying quantum correlations in mesoscopic condensed matter systems.
main_problem: The primary challenge is experimentally accessing and characterizing the two-electron coherences necessary to witness electronic entanglement in quantum circuits.
main_result: The authors introduce a photo-assisted tomography protocol that successfully reconstructs the two-electron Wigner distribution, revealing interaction-induced energy entanglement in quantum Hall edge channels.
method: The method uses routine transport measurements (dc-currents and current correlations) combined with an RF driving tone to encode off-diagonal two-electron coherences into measurable current responses.
model_or_system: The work focuses on electrons propagating in ballistic quantum conductors, specifically applying the protocol to Coulomb-coupled quantum Hall edge channels.
key_observables: Two-electron coherences ($G^{(2e)}_{AB}$), the two-electron Wigner distribution, and the violation of an entanglement witness based on Cauchy-Schwarz inequalities.
important_parameters: Coulomb interactions, thermal background, and the ability to resolve Wigner function negativities.
main_assumptions: The protocol assumes that the required measurements (average currents and current correlations) are routinely measurable in existing electronic interferometry setups.
figures_summary: Not specified, but the notes indicate the reconstruction of the two-electron Wigner distribution and the violation of the entanglement witness.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the concept of two-electron coherences and the entanglement witness, details the photo-assisted tomography protocol, applies it to Coulomb-coupled quantum Hall edge channels, and finally extends the approach to intra-channel coherences.
why_interesting: This work bridges advanced quantum optics measurement techniques (tomography, coherence reconstruction) directly into the study of strongly correlated electron systems in solid-state platforms, providing a concrete pathway to measure entanglement beyond simple charge measurements.
